title: Formless, beyond compare
hook: arupe hain, anupe hain: without form, beyond comparison (Jaap, chachari)

segments.voice: Yesterday, kripaal, namastvam kripaale, and your line, salute mercy. Did you let one small thing go? Today the rhythm changes again, and the lines get very short. Day three hundred thirty-nine.

Better than yesterday. Worse than her. Not as tall, as fast, as rich, as liked. Prettier than the old one. The mind is a measuring machine. It almost can't look at anything without setting it beside something else and checking which is bigger. A sunset gets compared to last week's. A child gets compared to a cousin. A few minutes of scrolling, and the comparisons pile up. And then a hymn says, in two words, that there is something nothing can be set beside. Today: formless, beyond compare.
screen: `BETTER THAN, WORSE THAN, NOT AS.` → `THE MIND IS A MEASURING MACHINE.` → `SOMETHING NOTHING CAN BE SET BESIDE.`

segments.voice: Further on, Jaap moves into a meter called chachari, and its lines are startlingly short. Each line is just two words. Aroop hain. Anoop hain. Ajoo hain. Abhoo hain. After the snake's long glide, it feels like quick footsteps, or a heartbeat. Hain means You are. So each line is a tiny sentence: You are this. Today, the first two, which the glide already saluted as aroope and anoope. Aroop: roop is form, shape, appearance, and the small a means without. You are formless. Nobody can paint You, sculpt You, put You on a screen. Sikhs take this seriously: there are no statues of God in a gurdwara, and the Guru Granth Sahib, a book of words, sits where you might expect an image. Then anoop. This one comes from upma, comparison, likeness. Anoop is the One with no likeness, nothing to compare to. And here the two words lean on each other. Comparison needs shapes. To say this is bigger than that, you need a this and a that, each with an outline. If the One has no form, there's nothing to measure against. Beyond compare isn't a boast that God wins every contest. It's that there's no contest at all. Now notice what that does for the measuring machine. Every morning, before the comparing starts, a Sikh reciting Jaap spends a few seconds saluting the one thing that can't be ranked. It's a small rest for the mind. A place where better than and worse than simply don't apply.
screen: `CHACHARI: TWO WORDS A LINE.` · `AROOP: WITHOUT FORM.` · `ANOOP: NOTHING TO COMPARE TO.` · `NO SHAPE, SO NO CONTEST.` · then, large: `BEYOND COMPARE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at something without comparing it. Pick one thing in front of you: a cup, a plant, your own hand, the sky in the window. Look at it for a while. Each time the mind says nicer than, older than, not as good as, notice it, smile at it, and come back to just this. This cup. This hand. Not better, not worse. Here. If you pray, you can say aroop hain, anoop hain softly. The bell holds the time.
Formless. Aroop hain, anoop hain: You are without form, and beyond compare, in the short, quick lines of Jaap's chachari meter.
Your line: beyond compare. Today, when you catch yourself measuring, someone else or yourself, stop at the word than, and leave the sentence unfinished. Day three hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite the short chachari lines of Jaap Sahib briskly each morning, and gurdwaras keep no images of God: the Guru Granth Sahib, a book of words, is the center.

fork.setup: your mind keeps measuring: better than, worse than. Jaap says the One is aroop and anoop. why can't the One be compared?
options: because the One always comes first.
because comparing needs shapes, and the One has no form.
fork.reveal: aroop, formless, and anoop, beyond compare, lean on each other: with no outline, there's nothing to set beside.

original.note: Gurmukhi: aroop, without form, from roop, form or appearance.

trapdoor: what you thought: formless means God is vague or invisible.
what it means: the One has no shape to picture and so nothing to be measured against.
what a scholar hears: anoop derives from upama, likeness; the chachari chhand packs each attribute into a two-word line ending in hain.

Everyday Punjabi use of anoop for 'wonderful, matchless': confirm.
